etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From しだらない (shidaranai).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From American English gasoline.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 兼ぬ (kanu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *kan-a-.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Sinitic.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 勞動 (MC law duwngX). 動 was replaced by kokuji 働 from 1897 onwards when the labour movement gained hold in Japan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 地位 (MC dijH hwijH). First cited in Japanese to a text from the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing from Chinese 地位 (dìwèi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tapu/ → /taɸu/ → */tawu/ → /tau/ → /tɔː/ → /toː/
From Middle Chinese 塔 (MC thap, “tower, pagoda, spire”).
An abbreviation for 卒塔婆 (sotoba, sotōba), a transliteration of Sanskrit स्तूप (stūpa, “heap”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: First appears in the Engishiki compilation of laws created in the early 900s, spelled phonetically in kanji as 阿良良伎. Spelled as 蘭, araragi literally means “wild onion” and refers to the wild rocambole, possibly hardneck garlic, notable for its tall green stalk sticking straight up. Used as a euphemism for 塔 (tafu at the time), as that word's Buddhist connotations were viewed as taboo in contexts having to do with the religious center of Itsuki no Miya (斎宮, also known as Saikū).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Found in the Kojiki of 712, and included in the Man'yōshū with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 須 (su). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *su.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 役 (MC ywek). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 役 (MC ywek).
The kan'on pronunciation, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨edati⟩ → /edat͡ɕi/
Noun form of the verb edatu and etatu.
From Old Japanese, itself of unknown derivative. Appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 役 (yaku, “service, work, role”) and 割り (wari), the noun form of 割る (waru, “to divide”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 後輩 (MC huwX|huwH pwojH, literally “back, behind + people of a certain kind; class, cohort”). Doublet of フベ (fube).
First cited to a text from 827 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 感 + する. The suru changes to zuru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 慣る (naru), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 所為 (MC srjoX hjwe|hjweH). The goon, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/sjowi/ → */sjoi/ → /ɕoi/ → /ɕei/ → /sei/ → /seː/
Probably a shift from shoi above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 所為 (MC srjoX hjwe|hjweH). The kan'on, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Min Nan reading só͘-ûi, Hakka só-vì.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 扇子.
First attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 日 (hi, “day”) + 帰り (kaeri, “return”). The kaeri changes to gaeri as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 果實 (MC kwaX zyit).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested from 13th century.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/moju/ → /mojeru/ → /moeru/
From classical verb 燃ゆ (moyu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Numerous derivatives already in use in the Heian period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 生 (MC sraeng|sraengH, “alive; fresh; raw; unprocessed”). The 漢音 (kan'on) reading, so likely a later borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Likely a contraction from 生き (iki, “life, living; freshness”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 生 (MC sraeng|sraengH). The 呉音 (goon) reading, so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Inherited from Old Japanese. There are various theories about the origin of this term, including:
* Apheresis of 生ふ (opu → pu → fu, “to grow”) used predicatively
* Contraction of 原 (paru → pu → fu, “field”)
* Contraction of 生ゆ (payu → pu → fu, “to grow”) used predicatively

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shinjitai simplified from 發.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift in pronunciation from older 真青 (masao), with gemination as an excrescence to express emphasis. First cited to the Nippo Jisho of 1603.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kwan/ → /kan/
From Middle Chinese 管 (kuɑn^X, “pipe, tube”).
The pipe sense is traced back to the writings of Zhuangzi, already an influential text in Japan in the 700s.
The brush handle sense is traced back to the text of the 詩経 (Shikyō, “Classic of Poetry”), an Old Chinese poetry anthology written from the 11th to 7th centuries BCE and already influencing Japanese writing since the mid-700s.
The wind instrument sense is sourced from the 延喜式 (Engishiki) of 927.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 管 (kuda, “pipe, tube”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 and the Man'yōgana of 759 with the ideogrammatic spelling of 小角 (literally “small horn”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 群 (MC gjun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 要求 (MC 'jiew gjuw).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/opu pu/ → /opopu/ → /ofofu/ → */owou/ → /oːu/
From the Old Japanese verb 覆(お)ふ (opu, “cover from above”) + ふ (-fu, auxiliary verb modifier, expressing repetition or ongoing state).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/urutapu/ → /uttafu/ → /uttaheru/ → /uttaeru/
Attested in the historical record since at least the early Heian period.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 訴ふ entry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 逆(さか) (saka).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 遊(あそ)ぶ (asobu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 酸(さん) (san, “acid”, also in 酸素 (sanso, “oxygen”, literally “acidic/sour element; sourstuff”)) + 化(か) (-ka, “-ization”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From earlier Old Japanese form 食(た)ぶ (tabu, “to (humbly) receive or get”, from a superior), a verb with the 下二段(しもにだん) (shimo nidan, “lower bigrade”) conjugation pattern. This was the humble form of 賜(た)ぶ, 給(た)ぶ (tabu, “to (deign to) give”, to an inferior), a verb with the full 四段(よだん) (yodan, “quadrigrade”) conjugation pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Most likely related to 給(たま)う (tamau, “to give”, as a superior gives a thing to, or does something for, an inferior).
Compare the historical development of meaning from “to humbly receive” → “to eat”, with the modern use of the humble verb 頂(いただ)く (itadaku, “to receive”) just before eating, in a sense of “I humbly receive this food.”
